subject: Throughput & streaming follow-up — Kilo pilot sizing
messages:
From: Kimberly Park <kimberly.park@redwood.com>
To: Alex Cho <alex.cho@kilo.ai>, Samantha Lee <samantha.lee@kilo.ai>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>, Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie.nguyen@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 16:03:00 -0700
Subject: Throughput & streaming follow-up — Kilo pilot sizing

Thanks again for a productive call this morning — quick recap and next steps so we have the same signal for sizing. I captured the numbers you gave and flagged a few clarifying asks below. I attached the workload snapshot you shared and a short SLO draft.

Recap (what we heard)
- Primary user path: customer chat assistant (short question + 400-500 token model completion).
- Average response length: ~420 tokens (median ~360; 95th ~780).
- Steady-state traffic: ~6 QPS (baseline daytime).
- Peak behaviour: recurring bursts tied to marketing pushes — observed spikes up to ~320 QPS for ~20–90s windows (you called these ‘peak moments’).
- Concurrent open streaming connections during peak: you estimated ~120 concurrent streams.
- Streaming expectation: progressive token-by-token playback; target perceived latency is p95 end-to-end < 200ms for first-chunk + continuous streaming (user should see the first ~32 tokens within ~150ms).

Sizing signals we’ll use
- Avg tokens per response: 420 tokens
- Steady tokens/sec ~= 6 QPS * 420 tokens = ~2,520 tokens/sec
- Peak tokens/sec ~= 320 QPS * 420 tokens = ~134,400 tokens/sec (short burst windows)

Clarifying asks (please confirm)
1) Are peak bursts typically concentrated in the US-East region (we heard yes) and do you have observed multi-region fanout?
2) For the concurrent streams number (~120), is that the number of concurrently active websocket connections or concurrent in-flight model invocations (some calls may multiplex multiple streams)?
3) Do you expect long-tailed session churn (i.e., many sessions staying open but idle) or do streams close quickly after generation finishes?

Next steps (our side)
- Rishi will produce an initial sizing workbook and two candidate configs: conservative baseline (low-cost steady) + aggressive burst pool (elastic GPUs + warm pool).
- I’ll share a short SLO draft (attached) mapping latency targets to rollout checks and fallback modes.
- If you can confirm questions 1–3 above and drop a week of request logs (anonymized) we’ll run a quick sample-based throughput sanity check.

Attachments: kilo_workload_snapshot_20260914.xlsx, redwood-slo-draft-20260914.pdf

Thanks — Kimberly

--
Kimberly Park
Enterprise Solutions | Redwood Inference
kimberly.park@redwood.com | +1 415-555-2781

From: Alex Cho <alex.cho@kilo.ai>

Cc: Samantha Lee <samantha.lee@kilo.ai>
Date: Tue, 14 Sep 2026 17:12:00 -07:00
Subject: Re: Throughput & streaming follow-up — Kilo pilot sizing

Kimberly — thanks for the recap, that matches our notes. Quick clarifications inline:

- Region: yes, the traffic triggering peaks is all US-East (east-1). We do have smaller EU spikes but those’re separate and lower scale.
- Concurrency: the ~120 number is concurrent open websocket connections during peak. Most calls open a single streaming websocket; there is minimal multiplexing.
- Stream lifecycle: streams close as soon as the generation completes. Idle/held-open sessions are rare for this product.

Additional details you can use for sizing:
- Typical user think-time inside the app between messages is ~9–18s.
- Average inbound prompt size: 60–80 tokens (so outbound dominates).
- During the largest marketing tests we saw sustained 60–90s periods where QPS averaged ~180 and had short peaks hitting ~320 for 30s.
- Concurrency during the largest tests spiked to ~210 websocket connections for the 30s peak windows (this is an upper-bound observed once).

We’ll upload one anonymized day of request logs to the Drive folder you linked. Let us know if CSV is fine (timestamp, req_id, seq_len_in, seq_len_out, region).

— Alex
Product Lead, Kilo.AI
alex.cho@kilo.ai

Subject: RE: Throughput & streaming follow-up — Kilo pilot sizing

Alex / Kimberly — digging into the numbers and the attachment quickly. A few first-pass observations and a conservative sizing sketch so the sales/ops team has something to discuss with Kilo this week. I attached an initial-sizing workbook with the scenarios below.

Assumptions used (from combined notes + sample snapshot)
- Model: mid-size open decoder (production latency/throughput profile similar to 70B quantized variant).
- Avg response tokens: 420
- Steady QPS: 6
- Peak burst short window avg: 180 QPS (sustained 60–90s), observed momentary peaks to 320 QPS for ~30s.
- Concurrent streams upper-bound: 210 (single observed test).

Sizing sketch (goal: keep p95 first-chunk <200ms, maintain continuous stream playback)
- Baseline (cost-optimized steady): 2 GPUs (H100 equivalent) with continuous batching and warm KV caching — should cover steady 6 QPS comfortably and absorb short small spikes to ~40–60 QPS with increased batching.
- Production baseline + burst pool: 4 GPUs baseline + elastic burst pool configured to add up to 12 additional GPUs on ~30s scale windows (warm pool with pre-warmed CUDA contexts). That layout gives comfortable headroom for the recurring 180 QPS sustained windows and handles 320 QPS short peaks with degradation strategy: canary fallback to slightly lower top-k or reduced sampling for burst windows to preserve latency SLO.
- Warm-pool considerations: pre-warming reduces cold-start token latency from ~800ms to <200ms for first-chunk on our infra. We recommend keeping a small warm pool (2 GPUs) in the same AZ as the US-East traffic.

Open risks / verification items
- We need a sample of the real request logs (CSV format Alex suggested) to validate tokens/sec distribution and tail behavior — the worst-case concurrency and 95th/99th response lengths matter a lot for burst sizing.
- Streaming enforcement: confirm whether client-side timeouts will close streams aggressively; if many clients keep connections open during backoff, concurrency impacts sizing more than QPS.

Proposed next steps
1) Kilo: upload a day of logs to the shared Drive (CSV with fields: timestamp, req_id, seq_len_in, seq_len_out, region).
2) Redwood (Rishi): run the sample-driven sizing job and return a recommended deployment plan + estimated cost delta (baseline vs burst).
3) Schedule a 30-minute follow-up Friday to review the workbook and pick a pilot config.

Attachment: initial-sizing-estimate-20260915.xlsx

If that looks reasonable I can convert the above into a short one-pager for procurement with the rough committed units and warm-pool timings.

— Rishi
Senior Performance Engineer | Redwood Inference
rishi.malhotra@redwood.com

Appreciate the quick turn — Alex
